props.title: That Thing You Do!
props.initialSlug: Small-town band's meteoric rise with one hit song

sections.content: Tom Hanks' directorial debut That Thing You Do! (1996) perfectly captures the meteoric rise and fall of a one-hit-wonder band during the Beatles-dominated 1960s. The film's genius lies in its pitch-perfect original song (written by Adam Schlesinger) that's catchy enough to believably become a hit, yet simple enough that we can watch it evolve from a ballad to an uptempo pop sensation. Like Almost Famous (2000) and Inside Llewyn Davis (2013), it explores the razor's edge between artistic integrity and commercial success, but with a lighter touch that makes its bittersweet elements hit even harder.

sections.content: The film's strength lies in its attention to period-perfect musical details, from the matching suits to the precise recreation of American Bandstand. Like Dreamgirls (2006) and Jersey Boys (2014), it shows how the music industry machinery could transform raw talent into polished product. But where those films lean into drama, That Thing You Do! maintains an infectious optimism even as the band's fate becomes clear. The Wonders' journey mirrors countless real bands of the era, making it both specific to its 1964 setting and universal in its storytelling.

Tom Everett Scott's Guy Patterson joins the ranks of great drummer characters in film, alongside J.K. Simmons' tormented student in Whiplash (2014) and John C. Reilly's Dale Doback in Step Brothers (2008). His transformation from jazz enthusiast to pop drummer illustrates the artistic compromises of commercial success, while Steve Zahn's guitarist and Liv Tyler's manager/girlfriend provide emotional anchors that ground the story's exploration of fame's impact on relationships. sections.content: That Thing You Do! sits comfortably alongside other films that capture pivotal moments in music history, like Good Morning, Vietnam (1987) and American Graffiti (1973). The film's recreation of mid-60s America shows the shift from regional scenes to national exposure through television, while Tom Hanks' Mr. White represents the corporate machinery that both enabled and constrained artistic expression. This tension between art and commerce would later be explored in grittier films like Control (2007) and 24 Hour Party People (2002).
